newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rescuers set to dig for hundreds buried in mud.
newsitem.headline: Peru rescuers set to dig for hundreds buried in mud.

text.p: Peruvian rescuers prepared to dig through mud on Thursday to continue searching for the bodies of an estimated 250 to 300 peasants buried after an Andean mountainside collapsed and swept away two villages.
But authorities feared many bodies would remain entombed in the up to 30 foot-(10 metre-) deep mud, despite the frantic work of rescuers using picks, shovels and their bare hands.
"It is most likely that many bodies are not going to be rescued," Civil Defence official and local Mayor Luis Barra Pacheco told Reuters.

President Alberto Fujimori said at the the disaster site that 41 bodies had been recovered by late on Wednesday, although an official at the local headquarters of the rescue operation had earlier put that figure at 47.
"This is a disaster with very serious consequences. It has literally buried two communities where there were approximately 100 families," Fujimori told local radio station Radioprogramas del Peru.
"We calculate that there are between 250 and 300 people buried under this immense amount of mud that we are seeing here."
The mountainside in southeastern Peru collapsed before dawn on Tuesday, burying the villages of Ccocha and Pumaranra at its foot with a torrent of mud, earth and rocks.

In the central square of nearby Kerapata, civil defence officials and forensic experts recorded details of the bodies brought in before sending them to a makeshift morgue in a schoolhouse in the neighbouring town of Tamburco.

"This one has lacerations on both feet," medical examiner Maria Navarrete Huaman told a civil defence worker jotting down the details she dictated. "We have 41 bodies so far and some parts of bodies -- arms, legs, extremities."
Tears streamed down the cheeks of Lucio Huaylla Velasquez as the magnitude of the disaster began to sink in. He lost his wife, 7-year-old daughter and 18-month-old son.

"First the terrorists kill us with guns and now this," he sobbed, referring to the guerrilla wars that have plagued Peru for the past 17 years. "I have nothing, not even a box to bury them in. There is no justice."

From a helicopter, the landslide looked like a wide brown gash on the face of the green mountainside. Roofs of the houses of what used to be Ccocha and Pumaranra poked through the mud. At the base of the mudslide, scores of rescuers were seen digging for bodies.

Dressed in mourning black, Dina Rivas Tapia stared up the hill from Kerapata's town square to the landslide, handkerchief in hand. "My entire family has disappeared. They were 25 people. I have no house, no money, I don't even have a bed."

Amid the tragedy, there were a few tales of heroism. When 14-year-old Alejandra Huallya Quispe heard a loud rumbling, she grabbed her sister and leapt out of the house. But her mother and another sister were crushed: "I jumped with my sister but the "huayco" (as mudslides are known locally) came and crushed my mother and other sister."
Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer warned of epidemic of diseases among the 250 to 600 families left homeless by the mudslide and other flooding and smaller slides in the area.
